Caspr is Analytical AI — purpose-built for business analysis, not conversation. Most AI tools generate plausible text. Caspr produces defensible conclusions, grounded in cited sources, structured the way a senior analyst would structure them.

The loop is simple. Type a single-line prompt — the market, the deal, the question you need answered. Caspr proposes a structured layout, the skeleton of your report, and asks a few clarifying questions to scope it precisely, the way an analyst scopes a brief before starting work. Confirm everything at the gate — depth, formats, language, price — and Caspr runs. What comes back is a boardroom-ready report — a fully cited PDF and, at the Business milestone, editable PPTX — with every insight linked to the source behind it.

Three stages make this possible. Assessment applies rigorous research methodology: it reasons through data and structures conclusions, rather than simply retrieving text. Sourcing draws on real-time data feeds, so the analysis reflects today's reality, not a training set frozen months ago. Behind both sit 25M+ curated, credible sources — documents, government databases, news feeds — not scraped web noise.

Generative AI writes. Analytical AI analyses. The difference shows up in the output: a report you can put in front of a board, an investor, or a client, where every number traces back to where it came from — not one you have to fact-check before you can trust it.

Start free with $100 Research Budget. No credit card required.

Your first analysis starts the moment you sign up — there is no setup wizard, no tour to click through. You land directly in the prompt box.

1. **Type your prompt.** One line is enough: name the subject, the market or geography, and the decision it needs to inform. For example, "Market size and key players in India's EV charging infrastructure market, for a Series B pitch."

2. **Submit.** Caspr reads the prompt and asks a short round of clarifying questions — scoping details it needs to target the report precisely, such as timeframe, geography, or the audience the report is for. Answer what you can; there is no wrong answer here, this step exists to catch gaps before any research runs.

3. **Review the layout.** Caspr proposes a structured layout — the report's table of contents, section by section, before a word is written. Add, remove, or reorder sections if you want to steer the output further. This is the scope you're actually paying for.

4. **Confirm at the gate.** One screen shows exactly what will be produced — depth, output formats, language, and style — all pre-set by Caspr, all changeable. On your very first run, before your account exists, the gate confirms scope only; price appears once you're signed up. From there, your first analysis draws on the $100 Research Budget your account starts with, so there's nothing to weigh.

5. **Confirm in chat.** Tell Caspr to generate and it runs. Generation is atomic — no pausing, no mid-run edits — so you can watch it build in Theater, or step away entirely. Turnaround depends on depth: a Brief usually lands in under 15 minutes, a Study within a couple of hours.

6. **Receive your report.** A boardroom-ready PDF, every insight cited to its source, ready to open the moment it lands.

That's the entire loop, start to finish, faster than a coffee break.

Run your first analysis now.

A strong prompt names three things: the subject, the market or geography, and the decision it needs to inform. You don't need a paragraph — one precise line beats five vague ones.

Weak: "Tell me about the fintech industry."
Strong: "Competitive landscape of B2B payments fintechs in Southeast Asia, for a market-entry decision."

A few examples across use cases:

- **Investor, deal sourcing:** "Market size and growth drivers for veterinary telehealth in the US, for an early-stage investment thesis."
- **Consultant, client deliverable:** "Business case for a mid-market grocery chain entering quick-commerce in Brazil."
- **Category manager:** "Competitive landscape and pricing benchmarks for private-label snacks in UK retail."
- **Corporate development:** "Acquisition targets in European industrial IoT, sub-$200M revenue."

Notice the pattern in every one: subject, geography, decision. That's what turns a general topic into a report someone can act on, rather than a summary of a Wikipedia page.

You will not get this wrong. If your prompt is thin — just an industry name, no geography, no stated purpose — Caspr asks clarifying questions before it runs anything. It scopes the gaps: which markets count as competitors, what timeframe matters, who the report is ultimately for. That round exists precisely so a one-line prompt is enough to start; you don't need to anticipate every detail up front.

The layout proposal that follows is your second checkpoint. Before any research runs, Caspr shows you the report's structure — the sections it intends to build — and you can add, remove, or reorder before confirming. Between the prompt, the clarifying questions, and the layout, there is no version of this where you're locked into the wrong report with no way back.

Try one of these prompts.

Submitting a prompt starts a short sequence, not an immediate report.

If your intent is ambiguous, Caspr first checks it with you — a quick confirmation before anything else runs. From there, you land on the **layout canvas**: the report's skeleton, sections laid out before any research runs, with a brief "Learning" wait while Caspr puts it together. Alongside it, in a drawer, Caspr asks a handful of **clarifying questions** — scoping details that sharpen the geography, timeframe, or angle of the analysis. You can add, remove, or reorder sections on the canvas, which is the main way you steer the final output, while answering the questions in the same view.

Both exist for the same reason: a full report is expensive to get wrong, and cheap to scope right. Confirming structure and intent up front is what makes the output boardroom-ready rather than a generic pass at your topic — and it's why you don't need to write a lengthy prompt to get a targeted result.

Next comes the **gate** — one screen confirming depth, formats, language, style, and price. Confirming in chat is what actually starts the run: tell Caspr to generate, and generation is atomic from that point — no pausing, no stopping, no mid-run edits. Turnaround depends on depth: a Brief typically lands in under 15 minutes, a Study within a couple of hours, Intelligence up to 24. You can watch it build in **Theater**, ask questions in the Ask Caspr drawer while you wait, or step away and come back to a finished PDF (and editable PPTX at Business).

What arrives is structured, cited, and ready to present — not raw notes to be cleaned up before anyone sees it.

See an example layout.

Because a senior analyst never starts writing before scoping the brief — and neither does Caspr.

A one-line prompt tells Caspr what you want to know. The clarifying questions tell it what you actually mean: which geography counts, which timeframe matters, what decision the report needs to support, who it's ultimately for. Skip that step and you'd get a generic report on a broad topic. Answer it, and you get one built for your specific question — the difference between a report that describes an industry and one that answers what you actually asked.

This is the assessment stage at work before the research even starts — targeting the analysis so the output is boardroom-ready on the first pass, not something you have to re-run three times to get right. It's also cheaper: a scoped report the first time costs less than a mis-scoped one you regenerate.

It takes seconds. A handful of short questions, then straight to the layout proposal and the gate. Nothing about this step spends your budget or slows you down in any meaningful way — it's the fastest checkpoint in the entire flow.

Answer and run.

Turnaround depends on depth. A **Brief**, built to answer one focused question, returns in around 15 minutes. A **Study**, Caspr's full analysis, takes 1–2 hours as it structures a complete report across market, competitive and strategic angles. **Intelligence**, the deepest depth, draws on the broadest sourcing, the most rigorous reasoning, and multiple models — so it runs longest, up to 24 hours, still a fraction of the weeks a comparable deep dive costs elsewhere.

Even at the top end, the comparison holds: a request that takes a research team or agency weeks to scope, research, draft and format arrives from Caspr the same day, cited and ready to present.

The process explains why speed doesn't come at the expense of rigour. You type a single-line prompt, Caspr proposes a structured layout, asks a few clarifying questions to sharpen scope, then runs — pulling from 25M+ curated sources and citing every insight along the way. No back-and-forth with an analyst, no waiting on someone else's calendar.

Your competitors are still waiting for the research.

Time it yourself — run one free.

A boardroom-ready report, roughly 100 pages, delivered as **PDF**. At the Business milestone, you also get an **editable PPTX** — the same report, restructured into slides you can adapt into your own deck and your own template.

Both formats carry every citation: click the red dot beside any insight and trace it to its source, without leaving the page. Neither is a rough draft. The PDF is finished, presentation-grade output — not raw research notes you need to clean up before anyone sees it. The PPTX exists for the exact moment you need to walk into a client meeting or a board session with the analysis already in your own format, not Caspr's.

Study and Intelligence depth reports also include XLSX, CSV, and Markdown in the base set, all delivered in your chosen language at no extra cost. Additional formats or languages beyond that base are available afterward from the Outputs tab, priced per output, whenever you need them.

Want to know what's actually inside those 100 pages — the sections, the exhibits, where the exec summary sits? That's covered separately.

See a sample report.

The $100 Research Budget is Caspr's free trial: $100 in gifted spend, no credit card, live for 90 days. It works exactly like a paid budget — a pool you draw down at fixed prices per analysis — except the balance is a gift, not a charge.

In runs, that is up to six Briefs at $15, or a full Study at $80 with room for a Brief or two alongside. A common first pass: one Brief to see how Caspr proposes a layout and asks clarifying questions, then a Study once the format has earned it. Intelligence, the deepest depth, sits above the trial — it unlocks at the Business milestone or can be bought à la carte for $399 — but everything below it covers the questions most people bring to Caspr first.

This is not a stripped-down demo. A Brief or Study run on trial spend is the identical analysis a paying customer receives: a structured layout, clarifying questions, then a boardroom-ready PDF or editable PPTX — a Brief in around 15 minutes, a Study within a couple of hours — every insight cited. Nothing is watermarked or truncated because it was paid for with gifted budget.

The point is proof. Run the market sizing you would otherwise brief a firm for $50,000 and three weeks. Check the citations. Judge whether it would survive your own board. Reports you generate stay in your account, readable and exportable, after the trial ends.

The one constraint is the clock: 90 days, then the unused balance expires — it does not roll into a paid budget. Spend it on a live question, not a hypothetical one.

Claim your $100 budget.

Start now — no card.

Start with a Study. For most questions it is the best first taste of the full product, and it sits in the middle of Caspr's three depths.

Depth is one axis, not three separate products. Every analysis draws from your Research Budget at a fixed price:

- Brief — $15. A quick, sourced answer to a single focused question. Use it to sample how Caspr works or to settle one specific point.
- Study — $80. A full market or competitive analysis: the structured, ~100-page report Caspr is built to produce. Most serious questions land here.
- Intelligence — $300 in-budget, or $399 à la carte. The deepest, board-grade deep dive, with broader sourcing and deeper reasoning. It unlocks at the Business milestone, or can be bought on its own with no subscription.

Pick by the decision in front of you. Checking a single fact or scoping a question — Brief. Sizing a market, mapping a landscape, building a business case — Study. A due-diligence screen or a board-level call where the stakes justify the depth — Intelligence.

Every depth returns the same core: a structured layout you confirm, clarifying questions, and a cited, boardroom-ready report — a Brief in around 15 minutes, a Study within a couple of hours, Intelligence up to 24. The difference is how far Caspr goes, not whether the output is boardroom-ready.

If you are not sure, run a Study. It shows you the full shape of a Caspr report, and your $100 trial budget covers one with room to spare.

Pick a depth and run.

Yes — and you should look before you run one blind. A live sample report is the fastest way to judge whether Caspr's output matches what you actually need, without spending any budget to find out first.

What you'll see mirrors exactly what a real run produces, because it is a real run — not a mockup built for marketing. The report opens with a cover and an executive summary that states the conclusion up front, in the way a senior analyst would open a briefing, rather than a table of contents promising conclusions somewhere later. From there it moves through structured sections built around the layout Caspr proposed from the original prompt: typically market sizing and definition, competitive positioning, trends and drivers, risks, and strategic implications, though the exact shape follows whatever the underlying question called for. Charts and tables carry the numbers; the narrative around them explains what the numbers mean for the decision at hand, not just what they are.

The detail worth paying closest attention to when you read a sample is the citation. Every factual insight in the report — a market size, a growth rate, a competitor's stated strategy, a regulatory shift — is shown next to the credible source it came from: a filing, a government database entry, a news report. This isn't a bibliography tacked on at the end of the document; it's inline, insight by insight, so any individual claim can be traced back and checked before it gets repeated in a room where someone will ask where the number came from. Walking through a sample report chapter by chapter and spot-checking two or three citations against their sources is the single fastest way to build confidence in the method, faster than reading any description of it.

Presentation quality is the other thing worth checking, because it's the part that's hardest to take on faith from a description. The sample is delivered in the same format a real analysis is: a boardroom-ready PDF or an editable PPTX, formatted to go directly into a deck rather than needing to be rebuilt by hand afterward. If your team's usual pattern after any research effort is 'now someone has to spend a day making this presentable,' that step is the one Caspr removes — and it's visible directly in the sample, not just claimed about it.

It's also worth reading a sample with an eye to scope, not just polish. Notice how narrowly or broadly the layout is built around the original question, and how the clarifying questions Caspr would have asked before the run shaped that scope. That's useful context for writing your own first prompt well — a tightly scoped question tends to produce a tighter, more useful report than a broad one.

Skeptical readers — an investor who's used to discounting glossy research decks, a consultant who's trained to poke holes in someone else's analysis — get more out of the sample than a casual skim. Pull one chart, trace its number back to the cited source, and check whether the source actually says what the chart claims. That single check, repeated two or three times across a report, tells you more about whether Caspr is trustworthy than any amount of description does. Pair that with the written and video accounts from analysts and researchers who've run their own reports, where available, for a second, independent read on whether the output holds up outside a controlled demo.

No login or spend is needed to browse the sample — it exists specifically so the decision to run your own analysis can be made with evidence already in hand, not on faith.

Reading a sample answers the two questions almost everyone actually has before they commit to running their own: does the structure hold up for a real business problem, and are the sources genuinely real and checkable. Once both of those hold up on someone else's question, running one on your own is the only way left to find out if it holds up on yours — and the cost of finding out starts at $15 for a Brief, a fraction of what a single hour with an outside analyst costs.
